standard.title: Ethics, security and sustainability in DT occupations
standard.description: analyse how people in design and technologies occupations consider ethical, security and sustainable factors to innovate and improve products, services and environments
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can analyse how people in design and technologies occupations consider ethical and sustainability factors when designing solutions (AC9TDE8K01). They can identify how designers respond to community needs and sustainability constraints. They have not yet analysed how ethical, security and sustainability factors combine to drive innovation, nor examined product life cycle thinking, mass production systems, or the role of global professional collaboration.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students analyse how people in design and technologies occupations integrate ethical, security and sustainability considerations — including product life cycle thinking, mass production ethics, and professional collaboration — to innovate and improve products, services and environments.

nodes.label: Product life cycle thinking
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain what product life cycle thinking is and how it influences design decisions.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain what product life cycle thinking means and give one example of how it has influenced a design decision (e.g. material choice, design for disassembly, re-use planning).
nodes.typical_width: Explain how life cycle thinking shifts decisions across the design process — material selection, production method, packaging, end-of-life — and give examples of products where life cycle thinking has produced a different design outcome than conventional approaches.
wider: Analyse the full product life cycle of a specific everyday object and identify where the greatest environmental impact occurs — explain what design change at that stage would have most effect
Compare a product designed with life cycle thinking (e.g. modular, repairable) with a conventional equivalent — evaluate the trade-offs for manufacturer, consumer and environment

Investigate how First Nations Australians' traditional production practices embody life cycle thinking — for example, the sustainable production and use of culturally significant pigments through calcination

response_modes.reason: Life cycle thinking is abstract without concrete examples. Multiple product cases — designed for disassembly, with lower-carbon material substitutions, and traditional sustainable practices — each make a different aspect of the concept visible. Students who see only one case often reduce it to recycling.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Comparing designed-for-life-cycle products with conventional equivalents is genuinely rich — the trade-offs are real and multi-sided, requiring analysis rather than description.
success_criteria: Correctly explains what product life cycle thinking considers beyond the point of sale
Gives a specific example of how it has influenced at least one design decision
nodes.hinge_reason: Life cycle thinking is the analytical framework used at N2, N3 and N4 — students who cannot apply it cannot evaluate mass production systems, professional design contributions, or the consequences of decisions through a sustainability lens.

nodes.label: Ethics and sustainability in mass production
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse ethics and sustainability considerations in mass production systems, including why manufacturers make different versions of the same product.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one ethical and one sustainability consideration in a mass production system; explain how each affects design or production decisions.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse a mass production system (e.g. food, clothing, electronics) — identify ethical considerations (labour, supply chain, intellectual property) and sustainability considerations (materials, waste, energy); explain why producers create different product versions and how product life cycle strategies affect these decisions.
wider: Examine the mass production of a food, clothing or footwear product — analyse the ethical and sustainability trade-offs at each stage of the production chain
Investigate what complete product life cycle strategies look like for a high-volume product and evaluate how realistic these are at scale
Compare how a multinational manufacturer and a small local producer of the same product type approach ethics and sustainability differently — explain the structural reasons for the differences
success_criteria: Identifies at least one ethical and one sustainability consideration in a specific mass production context
Explains how each consideration affects a production or design decision

nodes.label: Professional roles and global collaboration
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse how design and technologies professionals contribute to society and collaborate across global contexts.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe one design or technologies profession and explain how it contributes to society through at least one example project or outcome.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse the contributions of design and technologies professions — engineers, designers, technologists — to addressing societal needs; explain how factors such as time, finance, expertise and global manufacturing partnerships influence professional practice; examine at least one example of international collaboration.
wider: Analyse the collaboration between Australian and Vietnamese engineers on the Cao Lanh Bridge — identify what each party contributed and what made the collaboration necessary
Investigate how engineers working in disaster recovery or community energy access navigate ethical, sustainability and resource constraints simultaneously
Examine how rapid prototyping manufacturers in global supply chains change the relationship between Australian designers and production — evaluate the benefits and risks

response_modes.reason: Professional contributions are best understood through contrasting cases — local vs international, engineering vs design vs technology, disaster recovery vs commercial product development. Multiple contexts prevent students reducing 'contribution to society' to a single profession type.

success_criteria: Names a specific profession and connects it to a concrete societal contribution
Identifies at least one constraint (time, cost, expertise, geography) that shapes professional practice

nodes.label: Consequences of ethical and sustainability decisions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse the consequences of ethical and sustainability decisions for products, services and environments, including the accessibility of public environments and infrastructure.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe one consequence — intended or unintended — of an ethical or sustainability design decision for a product, service or environment.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how ethical and sustainability decisions in design produce consequences across users, environments and communities — including cases where decisions benefit some users while disadvantaging others; consider accessibility, safety, environmental impact and community outcomes.
wider: Analyse the design of a public environment (e.g. managed public space, road corridor) for its accessibility, sustainability and safety — evaluate how competing design goals were balanced
Examine the design of infrastructure to reduce fire risk in rural communities — identify what ethical, sustainability and safety decisions shaped the design and what the consequences were
Investigate an instance where a design decision improved sustainability but reduced accessibility or vice versa — evaluate how the trade-off should have been managed

response_modes.reason: Consequence analysis requires students to reason forward from decision to outcome to affected party — without this scaffold, students describe what was decided rather than analyse what followed. The reasoning chain (decision → mechanism → consequence → who is affected and how) is the key skill.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Public infrastructure and fire-risk community design cases are rich because consequences are multi-sided and real — they require students to weigh competing values and interests rather than identify a single correct outcome.
success_criteria: Identifies a specific ethical or sustainability decision and names at least one concrete consequence
Explains the mechanism connecting the decision to the consequence (not just stating both)
